questions.prompt: What is consensus in a distributed system?

options.text: Encrypting data across nodes
Getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value or ordered sequence despite failures
Splitting data across nodes
Caching results near users

questions.explanation: Consensus is agreement on one value (or sequence) among nodes even when some fail — the basis for leader election, atomic commit, and replicated state machines.

questions.prompt: A consensus cluster of 2f+1 nodes can tolerate how many node failures?

options.text: 2f failures
f failures, while still having a majority
All of them
Zero failures

questions.explanation: With 2f+1 nodes, a majority (f+1) survives f failures. For example, 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures and still form a quorum of 3.

questions.prompt: Why do consensus clusters typically run an ODD number of nodes?

options.text: Odd numbers are faster
A majority of an odd set tolerates the most failures per node; e.g. 4 nodes tolerate only 1 failure, the same as 3, for more cost
Even numbers can't form a majority at all
It has no effect

questions.explanation: 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures, but 4 nodes tolerate only 1 — the same as 3 — so the extra even node adds cost without extra fault tolerance.

questions.prompt: How does Raft elect a leader?

options.text: The node with the lowest IP always wins
A follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate, increments the term, requests votes, and wins with a majority
A human administrator picks it
The oldest node is always leader

questions.explanation: On an election timeout, a follower becomes a candidate for a new term and requests votes; winning a majority makes it leader, and it then sends heartbeats.

questions.prompt: What does the FLP impossibility result tell us?

options.text: Consensus is impossible in all systems, always
In a fully asynchronous system where one node may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee it always reaches consensus
Networks never fail
Quorums are unnecessary

questions.explanation: FLP shows consensus can't be guaranteed under full asynchrony with a possible crash. Real systems use timeouts (partial synchrony) and sometimes randomization to make progress.

questions.prompt: Should you implement your own distributed leader election with a database flag?

options.text: Yes, it's simple and correct
No — it can produce split brain under a partition; use a consensus-backed coordination service like etcd or ZooKeeper
Yes, as long as the database is fast
No, leader election is never needed

questions.explanation: A homegrown flag lacks the majority-overlap guarantee, so a partition can create two leaders (split brain). Use a proven coordination service that provides quorum-based election.
